title: Check yourself: executors and thread pools

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A report pool is built as `new ThreadPoolExecutor(4, 16, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(500))`. Fifty slow reports are handed to it within a second, and none has finished yet. How many threads is the pool running?

options.text: Sixteen, since reports past the core size start new threads up to the maximum, and only after that wait in the queue
options.says: past the core size a task goes into the queue first; extra threads start only when the queue refuses it

options.text: Four, since threads past the core size start only after a core thread has been idle for the keep-alive time
options.says: the keep-alive time decides when idle threads past the core end, not when threads start

options.text: Sixteen, since a queue of 500 is meant for quiet hours, so the pool starts threads up to its maximum when work arrives in a burst
options.says: the pool has no notion of a burst; with room in the queue, every report past the core waits there

options.text: Four, since reports past the core size wait in the queue, and threads past the core start only when the queue is full
options.says: with 46 of 500 places taken the queue never refuses, so no thread past the core starts

origin.section: A Pool Queues Before It Grows: Threads Past the Core Start Only When the Queue Is Full

questions.stem: A nightly job loops over 500 accounts and calls `pool.submit(() -> reconcile(account))` on a fixed pool, keeping none of the returned values. Reconciling three of the accounts throws `IllegalStateException`. The application has no uncaught-exception handler of its own. What does the log show about those three?

options.text: No trace of them, since each exception is stored where only a later get() call would bring it out
options.says: submit() runs the task inside a FutureTask, which stores the exception in the Future; only get() would have thrown it

options.text: No trace of them, since a pool's worker catches each task's exception and drops it, so it can go on to the next task
options.says: a pool's worker doesn't catch task exceptions: one from execute() ends the worker and is printed; here the FutureTask caught it

options.text: Three stack traces, since an exception that leaves a task reaches the default handler of the pool thread that ran it
options.says: that is what execute() does; with submit() the exception never leaves the FutureTask

options.text: Three stack traces, since the pool's afterExecute hook prints each exception that a task throws on one of its threads
options.says: the default afterExecute does nothing, and for a submitted task it receives null

origin.section: execute() Hands a Task's Exception to the Thread; submit() Keeps It in the Future

questions.stem: A shutdown hook runs `pool.shutdown(); dataSource.close();`. At that moment one export task is running and 40 are waiting in the pool's queue, and every task writes to the database. What happens to the 40?

options.text: They are dropped without running, since shutdown() clears the queue and leaves only the running export to finish
options.says: shutdown() keeps the queued tasks and runs them; only shutdownNow() hands them back unrun

options.text: They run and fail, since shutdown() returns while they are still queued, and they reach the database after dataSource.close()
options.says: shutdown() doesn't wait; the queued tasks run after it returns, against the closed data source

options.text: They are dropped without running, since a pool whose shutdown has begun refuses every task that has not yet started
options.says: shutdown() refuses tasks submitted after it, not those already in the queue

options.text: They run and succeed, since shutdown() returns only once the queued tasks have run, before the hook reaches dataSource.close()
options.says: shutdown() returns at once; waiting is awaitTermination's job

origin.section: shutdown() Stops Intake, Not Work: Wait for It With awaitTermination()

questions.stem: A service calls a geocoding vendor from `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20)`. The vendor's contract allows 20 calls in flight and answers 429 beyond that. The team moves the calls to `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`. A burst of 300 lookups arrives. What does the vendor see?

options.text: Up to 20 calls at once, since the JVM gives the virtual threads as many carrier threads as the old pool had
options.says: the carriers are not sized to the old pool, and a virtual thread waiting on the network gives its carrier up, so they cap nothing here

options.text: Up to 300 calls at once, since each lookup gets a thread of its own, and no lookup waits for a free one
options.says: the pool of 20 was the only limit, and the move removed it; the calls themselves need a limit such as a Semaphore

options.text: Up to 20 calls at once, since the new executor keeps the pool size the service configured before the move
options.says: the virtual-thread executor has no pool size; it starts one thread per task

options.text: Up to 300 calls at once, since each lookup gets a carrier thread of its own for as long as its call lasts
options.says: the count is right but the reason isn't: a virtual thread waiting on the network gives its carrier up, which is why waiting costs almost nothing

origin.section: A Pool's Size Is Also a Limit on Concurrency, and Some Executors Have None

concepts: A fixed pool's size also limits how many calls reach a downstream at once; the cached pool and the virtual-thread executor have no such limit, so the call itself needs one.
newFixedThreadPool queues without a limit, so work that arrives faster than it is done waits in memory until the heap runs out.
